questions.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to two-fifths of the rate of increase of the diameter. Determine the radius of the circle at that moment.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{D}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{2}{5} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{4}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2r & =\frac{4}{5\pi } \\ r & =\frac{2}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{D}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{1}{\pi }.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to two-thirds of the rate of increase of the circumference. What is the radius of the circle at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{2}{3} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C=2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\frac{4\pi }{3} \\ r & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the ink blot is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=10,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=4\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=10\,\text{mm},$ $C=2\pi (10)=20\pi \text{ mm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=4\pi $ and $C=20\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi \cdot \frac{20\pi }{2\pi } \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =40\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area is increasing at a rate of $40\pi {\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=12\pi .$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=12\pi $ and $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3,$ and solve for $r.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}12\pi  & =3\cdot 2\pi r \\ 12\pi  & =6\pi r \\ r & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius at that moment is $2\text{ m}.$

questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=5,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-8\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=5\,\text{cm},$ $C=2\pi (5)=10\pi \text{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-8\pi $ and $C=10\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{10\pi }{2\pi } \\ -8\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 5 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{8\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{8\pi }{5}\text{ cm/s}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095273/assets/5bf71c5c613c69263e15137bbd5aa56716a8c289a4457a95a9c7b1fddd8af03b.png)

A spherical balloon is inflated at the rate of $18{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ If at a particular moment the balloon's radius is changing at the rate $\frac{1}{2\pi }\text{ cm/s},$ then what is the radius of the balloon at this moment? Do not round the answer.

$r=$
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=18{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s},
$$

and we want to find $r$ when $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\text{ cm/s}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=18$ and $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{2\pi },$ and solve for $r.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 18 & =2{r}^{2} \\ r & =\sqrt{9} \\ r & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius at that moment is $3\text{ cm}.$

A spherical soap bubble is expanding, causing its enclosed volume to increase at a rate of $24\pi \text{ }{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius increasing at the moment when the radius is $3\text{ }\text{cm}?$ Do not round the answer.

The radius of the bubble is increasing at a rate of 
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the bubble and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=24\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=3\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the volume of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=24\pi $ and $r=3,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (3)^{2} \\ 24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 36\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when the radius is of the bubble is $3\,\text{cm},$ the radius is increasing at a rate of  $\frac{2}{3}$ $\text{ }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$

\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =1\cdot 4\pi (2)^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the balloon is increasing at a rate of $16\pi {\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}$
 when the radius is $2\,\text{cm}.$

questions.problem: A snowball is rolling down a snow-covered hillside. At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the sphere is numerically equal to three times the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the sphere at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the sphere, $V$ the volume of the sphere, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =12\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(12\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =144\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =144\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095273/assets/2ef2330edb3a3822e6edd8bd443238d027e45e1a8b12ceb8b6be53f9fa68fbd7.png)

A large latex balloon is inflated with helium so that its radius increases at a rate of $3\,\text{in/s}.$ How fast is the volume of the balloon increasing at the moment when the radius is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{in}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3\,\text{in/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=\frac{3}{2}\,\text{in}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $r=\frac{3}{2},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot 4\pi {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =27\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the balloon is increasing at a rate of $27\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/s}$
when the radius is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{in}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Related Rate With a Circle
canonical_examples.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to half the rate of increase of the circumference. What is the radius of the circle at that moment?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A = \pi r^2,$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A =  \pi r^2 =  \pi \left(\dfrac{C}{2\pi} \right)^2 = \dfrac{C^2}{4\pi}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C = 2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\pi  \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A circular oil spillage is being cleaned up by a team using specialized cleaning equipment. If the area of the circle is *decreasing* at a rate of $6\pi\,\text{m}^2/\text{h}$, what is the rate at which the radius is decreasing at the instant when the radius is $2\,\text{m}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095273/assets/d769569ed7854f4d6eb085853b51eb0e5aab0e14cfc3bcdf1e5a480d996ccc9e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=2,$ and we are also told that  $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = -6\pi.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} = -6\pi$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (2) \\ -6\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius is decreasing at a rate of $\dfrac{3}{2}$ meter per hour.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Related Rate With a Sphere: Word Problem
canonical_examples.problem:
Air is leaking from a spherical balloon at the rate of $500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius of the balloon decreasing when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095273/assets/460fd4059be2c655e01b89db2738225a50578b5c76bbe048f83312f0bff655ec.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}$ when $r=10\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi$ and $r=10,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-500\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (10)^{2} \\ -500\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 400\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{5}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the balloon is decreasing at a rate of $1.25\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}.$
